title: Saying no — one word for everything
goal: Master Estonian negation, which turns out to be **simpler than English** and far simpler than Finnish.
bekal: negate any verb for any person with a single word: *ei*
use *ära* to forbid and *mitte* to negate things other than verbs

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kadunud telefon
dialogs.intro: In the campus cafeteria. Budi is patting his pockets in a panic.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kerli, ma ei leia oma telefoni.
lines.id: Kerli, I can't find my phone.
lines.literal: Kerli, I not find own phone-part.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ei ole. Ma ei näe seda kuskil.
lines.id: No. I don't see it anywhere.
lines.literal: not is. I not see it-part anywhere.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hea mõte. Aga ma ei mäleta numbrit.
lines.id: Good idea. But I don't remember the number.
lines.literal: good thought. but I not remember number-part.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: You don't remember your own number?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ei mäleta. Keegi ei mäleta enam numbreid.
lines.literal: not remember. anyone not remember anymore numbers-part.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: See on tõsi. Mina ka ei mäleta.
lines.literal: that is true. I also not remember.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Wait. I feel something in my pocket.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah... see on siin. Kogu aeg.
lines.id: Yes... it's here. The whole time.
lines.literal: yes... it is here. whole time.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Sa ei ole esimene ega viimane.
lines.id: You're not the first and not the last.
lines.literal: you not are first nor last.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm not telling anyone about this.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ei ole. Ma olen aus sõber.
lines.id: No, I'm not. I'm an honest friend.
lines.literal: not is. I am honest friend.

notes: **Count how many times *ei* appears in this dialogue, then notice that it never changes.** *Ma ei leia*, *sa ei mäleta*, *keegi ei mäleta*, *mina ei luba* — one word for six people. Compare Finnish, which has six different forms (*en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät*).

⚠️ **The verb doesn't change for the person either.** *Ei mäleta* works for I, you, he/she, we, you (plural) and they. So the Estonian negative actually takes **less memorizing** than the ordinary form.
**Ei ole = pole.** Both are correct and equally common. *Pole* is slightly more casual. *Mul pole aega* = *mul ei ole aega* = I don't have time.
**Ära muretse, ära ütle.** *Ära* is used only to forbid. It **can't** be replaced by *ei*: "ei muretse" means "doesn't worry", not "don't worry".

grammars.title: Ei — and a one-line rule for forming it
body: Negating an Estonian verb takes two steps, and the second step has a perfect shortcut.

head: "ma" form
Drop -n
Negative
Works for
rows: I, you, he/she, we, you (pl.), they

after: **The rule: take the *ma* form, drop the *-n*, put *ei* in front.** There are no exceptions to remember at A1. This is one of the cleanest rules in the whole Estonian language.
This shortcut is one more reason to memorize the *ma* form of every new verb, as recommended in unit 10. That one form gives you the other five **and** the whole negative.

⚠️ **After a negative, the object switches to the partitive.** *Ma loen raamatu* (I read the book to the end) → *ma ei loe raamatu**t***. *Mul on auto* → *mul ei ole auto**t***. This rule is covered in full in unit 13; for now, just notice that the ending shifts.

grammars.title: Three other negators, and when to use each
body: *Ei* handles verbs. The three words below handle the rest.
after: ⚠️ **Ära and ei can't be swapped.** *Sa ei tule* = you aren't coming (a statement). *Ära tule* = don't come (a command). English separates them too — "you don't" versus "don't!" — so your instinct is already right; only the words are new.
*Mitte* is used when what you negate isn't a verb: *mitte mina* (not me), *mitte siin* (not here), *mitte kunagi* (never), *mitte veel* (not yet).
Prohibitions you'll often see on signs: *Ära suitseta!* (No smoking), *Ärge puudutage!* (Do not touch), *Sissepääs keelatud* (No entry).

sections.title: Negative words — and the double negative

blocks.title: ⚠️ The double negative is REQUIRED
items: *Ma ei tea midagi.* — literally "I don't know nothing". Two negatives in one sentence, and that's the **correct** form.
Dropping one of them gives you a wrong sentence. "Ma tean midagi" means "I know something" — the opposite meaning.
Many languages work this way — Spanish *no sé nada*, French *je ne sais rien*, Russian *я ничего не знаю*. Standard English is the odd one out.
English says *I don't know anything*, not *I don't know nothing*. In Estonian, the "nothing" version is exactly what you want — so forget what your English teacher told you, just this once.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Estonians say no directly, and that isn't rude.** A plain *ei* counts as an honest answer that respects the other person's time. Cushioning a refusal with three layers of small talk can come across as hesitation or even insincerity. If you mean no, say no.

blocks.title: Pole — the short form you'll hear constantly
items: *pole* = *ei ole*. *Mul pole aega.* — I don't have time.
*Pole viga.* — No problem. (literally: "there's no flaw") ⚠️ It's also the answer to an apology.
*Pole tänu väärt.* — Don't mention it. (literally: "not worth thanks")

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with ei, ära or mitte.
Put the words in the right order.

answers.0: Ma ei ole kodus. — Sa ei lähe kooli. — Ta ei tea. — Me ei söö. — Te ei räägi eesti keelt. — Nad ei tule.
answers.1: ei — Ära — Mitte — ei — Ära — ei
answers.2: Ma ei tea midagi. — Keegi ei tea. — Ma ei käi seal kunagi. — Mul ei ole aega. — Ära muretse! — Ei, aitäh.
answers.3: Ma ei tea midagi. — Keegi ei tea. — Ära muretse. — Mul pole aega. — Ei, aitäh.
